extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (patent owners, challengers, and IP litigators) considering or handling Ex Parte Reexamination (EPRx)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative considerations for requesting, defending, timing, and litigating ex parte reexamination (EPRx) proceedings before the USPTO, including differences with IPRs, statistical outcomes, and tactical steps for patent owners and challengers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Ex Parte Reexamination (EPRx)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tool that allows a party to request that the Patent Office reexamine an already-granted patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to challenge granted patents based on patents and printed publications; forms the baseline for deciding whether to pursue reexamination versus other forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art that can be leveraged in EPRx
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents and printed publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPRx is limited to prior art in the form of patents and printed publications (i.e., not other types of evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who can file a reexamination request
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone (third party, patent owner); third party can file anonymously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both patent owners and third parties may initiate EPRx; anonymity can be strategically important for challengers seeking to avoid triggering litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold for ordering reexamination (SNQ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial new question of patentability (SNQ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CRU orders reexamination only if the request raises a substantial new question of patentability relative to the patent as granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party participation after initial request
rubrics_metrics.description: Can third parties participate after initial request: Generally no.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the reexamination is underway, challengers typically cannot actively participate in the substantive proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who conducts reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners in Central Reexamination Unit (CRU).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CRU examiners handle EPRx merits, and their practices (e.g., what art they consider) shape proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal route for EPRx decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal CRU’s decision to PTAB → Appeal PTAB’s decision to CAFC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-reexamination appeals follow the PTAB and Federal Circuit appellate route; appeals add time and can be used strategically.

rubrics_metrics.name: No estoppel for challengers
rubrics_metrics.description: No estoppel created (preserve prior art-based invalidity defenses for other forums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challengers retain the ability to raise prior-art invalidity defenses in later proceedings because EPRx does not create IPR-style estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPRx availability when IPR is not available
rubrics_metrics.description: EPRx available when IPR is not (e.g., after 1-year from complaint filing, after prior non-instituted IPR challenge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPRx can be used in temporal or procedural windows where IPR is barred or unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: No word limits in EPRx filings
rubrics_metrics.description: No word limits → more robust challenges and larger # of SNQs possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions can present many grounds and extensive argumentation without the strict page/word constraints typical of IPR petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower standard to raise a challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower standard for raising a challenge (compared to IPRs, D. Ct.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because EPRx is ordered on an SNQ standard rather than the IPR institution standard, it can be easier to initiate reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential to reduce or eliminate damages (intervening rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential to reduce or eliminate damages (intervening rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reexamination can affect infringement remedies and damages depending on claim amendments and intervening rights doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased likelihood of stay pending reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Increased likelihood of stay pending reexamination (given accelerating timelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may be more likely to stay district-court proceedings early in litigation if EPRx is pending, especially when timelines show likely resolution before trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenger limitation: no participation after filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent challenger generally cannot participate in the reexam after filing of initial request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits challengers' ability to respond to amendments or newly added claims during prosecution, ceding procedural control to patent owner and examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent owner can amend or add claims during EPRx
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Owner can readily amend and add claims during reexamination – whose patentability cannot be challenged by the patent challenger (in the EPRx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners commonly add claims; challengers cannot directly contest the patentability of newly-added claims within the same EPRx proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims may emerge from reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: Although large majority of reexam requests are granted, some claims of the patent generally emerge from reexam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical statistics show a substantial proportion of reexams result in claims surviving in some form (confirmed or amended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of discretionary denial under 35 U.S.C. § 325(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if SNQ exists, there is still a possibility of 325(d) discretionary denial (e.g., if the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments were previously presented to the USPTO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests can be denied on discretionary grounds when issues overlap prior proceedings; counsel should evaluate whether 325(d) applies before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easier amendments for patent owners vs IPRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Easier to amend or add claims during EPRx (compared to IPRs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners can commonly add a larger volume of claims and obtain entry of amendments more readily than in IPR proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common early large-volume claim additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Common for Patent Owners to add large volume of claims before first office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing preliminary amendments or many new claims early is a frequent owner tactic to reshape claim scope and create fallback positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to initiate EPRx during pending IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to initiate reexamination during a pending IPR – especially when things are not going well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel filings may be used tactically; timing and estoppel interplay with IPR must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner control over which art CRU evaluates
rubrics_metrics.description: Control which art is substantively evaluated by CRU during reexamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners can influence the record (e.g., via reexam request framing and IDS behavior), and CRU may limit consideration to art/grounds raised in the request.

rubrics_metrics.name: CRU may not consider art beyond reexam request
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when IDSs including art is submitted during reexaminations, CRU may not consider any art/ground other than what’s raised in reexam request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits scope of examiner consideration to the specific art/arguments presented in the request, affecting challenger and owner strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-initiated EPRx can strengthen patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-initiated EPRx challenge can strengthen patent against subsequent challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners may use EPRx proactively to preemptively amend/clarify claims and create prosecution history to deter or withstand later attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader claim interpretation standard (BRI) risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Jeopardizes validity of issued patent, given broader claim interpretation standard (BRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPRx applies broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI), which may increase vulnerability of claims compared to district court claim construction standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentage of cases with un-amended claims emerging
rubrics_metrics.description: On average, in 20% of reexams, challenged claims emerged in un-amended form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners face non-trivial risk that original claims will survive without amendment; challengers should not assume complete cancellation is likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced damages concern for owners
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced damages (intervening rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments or reexamination outcomes can limit available damages for past infringement via intervening rights doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative concern by remaining patent life
rubrics_metrics.description: Lesser concern for patents with longer life remaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners may be less worried about damaged damages recovery or intervening-rights effects for patents with substantial remaining term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty about intervening rights for newly added claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Open question about intervening rights for newly added claims (absolute v. equitable intervening rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic calculus must account for unsettled law on remedies for newly-added claims in reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: High grant rate for EPRx requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Over 90% of EPRx requests are granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPRx institution/grant rate is substantially higher than IPR institution rates (~67%), making initiation statistically successful in getting an exam.

rubrics_metrics.name: CRU decision timing statutory requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The CRU must decide on a request within 3 months (see 35 U.S.C. § 303).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institution decision is theoretically prompt; compare to ~6-7 months for IPR institution timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical EPRx outcomes distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Range of outcomes: some claims confirmed, cancelled, or changed; historical averages and FY2023 snapshot provided (e.g., All Claims Confirmed / All Claims Cancelled / Claims Changed percentages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although many requests are granted, 'winner-take-all' outcomes are becoming more common and results vary year-to-year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall EPRx timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: It may take 2-3 years to conclude an ex parte reexamination and related appeals; median time to reexamination certificate is roughly 20 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB and Federal Circuit appeals, remands, rehearing requests, and other procedural events can extend timelines substantially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenger timing advantage: file sooner
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Patent Challenger, filing sooner is often better: increased chance of a reexamination certificate before parallel proceedings are concluded; likelihood of a stay increases at early stages of litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early filing may maximize tactical benefits like stays and preemptive effect on damages or litigation posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner timing tactics: opportunities to delay
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Patent Owner, there are often opportunities to delay: waiting out the 2-month Patent Owner Response period and Office Action response periods; PTAB appeal; requesting Reconsideration after a PTAB appeal decision; Fed. Circuit Appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners can leverage procedural mechanisms to extend enforcement or postpone final adverse outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to leverage EPRx after IPR denial (challenger view)
rubrics_metrics.description: If institution denied in IPR, consider timing relative to co-pending litigation; how receptive the court is to stay; reason for denial (was the IPR denied due to perceived deficiency in presented art or ground?); whether new art is needed; whether the same art is being presented in a new light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPRx may be appropriate when denials stem from presentation issues and new art can address deficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remaining enforceable life as a strategic consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Remaining enforceable life of patent: e.g., patents nearing expiration may be particularly good candidates for challengers; expired patents cannot be amended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life remaining affects the value of pursuing EPRx for both challengers (to reduce damages) and owners (to avoid losing enforcement value).

rubrics_metrics.name: No co-pending litigation: estoppel and anonymity benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike IPR, EPRx filing does not trigger any estoppel; challengers can request reexamination anonymously, thereby potentially avoiding a litigation being triggered against them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes EPRx attractive for discreet challenges or when litigating would be undesirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost considerations for EPRx
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost: EPRx are less expensive for challengers and can also be prepared inexpensively by Patent Owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduced cost relative to other forums can make EPRx an economical choice; limited challenger participation also lowers costs but cedes control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff: limited challenger participation saves cost but cedes control
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost no participation allowed by challengers (saves cost, but cedes control).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challengers must accept reduced ability to shape prosecution if they value cost savings and anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future-proofing value of EPRx
rubrics_metrics.description: Future proofing: Claims emerging are going to be more inoculated from future challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners can use EPRx to strengthen claims proactively, making later invalidity challenges more difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: When owner considers EPRx after IPR institution
rubrics_metrics.description: If IPR institution granted (Patent Owner considering EPRx): consider strength of petition and amendment considerations; limited amendments possible in IPR, whereas larger number of amendments may be entered in EPRx; no requirement to wait until final decision in IPR before filing EPRx; timing if amended or new claims issue after IPR bar date, no IPR challenge possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners should weigh parallel proceedings, amendment opportunities, and timing relative to IPR bar dates and damages impact when deciding to pursue EPRx.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider damages impact of potential amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Is damages impact from potential amendments palatable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners must evaluate whether narrowing or changing claims during EPRx will materially reduce infringement damages or enforcement leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate for discretionary denial under 35 U.S.C. § 325(d) (owners before first OA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even before grant, consider advocating for discretionary denial under 35 U.S.C. § 325(d) if the facts support it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners can push for denial where issues substantially overlap prior art/arguments previously before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited 325(d)-only petitions often allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: While outside the rules, a petition is now commonly allowed if limited to 325(d) issues (e.g., does not argue against the SNQs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrow petitions focused on discretionary denial theories can be an effective pre-grant tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request waiver under 37 C.F.R. § 1.183 to suspend entry rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Owner should request a waiver, under 37 C.F.R. § 1.183, to suspend the rules that would otherwise disallow entry of a petition (37 C.F.R. §§ 1.530(a) and 1.540).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative waivers can be used to preserve procedural options that might otherwise be foreclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requester opposition period
rubrics_metrics.description: Requester is given a 2-week period to submit an opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing constraints around initial oppositions influence pre-institution tactical choices by owners and challengers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider preliminary amendment if reexamination is ordered
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reexamination is ordered, consider a preliminary amendment, at least to add new claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early amendments can create fallback positions and shape the initial examination record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider not filing a patent owner statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider not filing a patent owner statement, because filing one gives the requester a chance to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a statement can permit challenger reply; declining may avoid creating additional responsive briefings but has tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start response preparation early after first Office Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Start preparing the response early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners should be ready to act within short response windows and should avoid last-minute responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2-month response period and limited extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: 2-month response period and usually no extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners must meet tight deadlines post-office action; planning is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amend at the first Office Action; add narrowing new claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Take advantage of the opportunity to amend claims: amend at the first Office Action, rather than waiting; even if maintaining the original claims, add amended versions as new claims; add new claims (must be narrowing compared to original claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early, narrowing amendments can preserve rights and present fallback claim sets to the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make use of examiner interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Make use of examiner interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews can speed resolution, clarify examiner positions, and improve chances of favorable amendments being entered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide declaration evidence when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide declaration evidence when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits/declarations can support patentability positions, rebut art, or establish facts relevant to claim amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider claim construction positions carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider claim construction positions: careful construction is often how patent owners distinguish prior art without amending the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic claim construction in the prosecution record can sometimes avoid amendments and preserve damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep an eye toward PTAB appeal and set up a supportive record
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep an eye toward PTAB appeal; set up a record that can support reversal or remand if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserving arguments, evidence, and procedural positions in the record is important for potential appeals.
